sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go has become the dominant language for writing microservices. Its fast startup time, tiny memory footprint, and single-binary deployment make it ideal for containerised, horizontally-scaled services. Interviewers at companies running Kubernetes-based platforms expect Go engineers to understand not just how to write a service, but how services discover each other, how failures cascade, and how you trace a request across ten hops.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Decompose a monolith into microservices along domain boundaries (DDD bounded contexts). Each service owns its data store, communicates via well-defined interfaces (gRPC or REST), and is independently deployable. In Go, a service is typically a main package that wires together transport (net/http or grpc), business logic (pure Go types), and infrastructure (database, cache). Go kit layers these concerns explicitly; go-micro adds service registry and RPC. The service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) handles mTLS and retries transparently at the sidecar level.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Decomposition: single-responsibility per service, data isolation, API versioning. 2. Go kit: endpoint/transport/service layers, middleware chain for logging and metrics. 3. Service discovery: client-side (Consul + go client) vs. server-side (Kubernetes Service + kube-dns). 4. Circuit breaker: half-open state, sony/gobreaker, hystrix-go; fail-fast to avoid cascade. 5. Distributed tracing: OpenTelemetry Go SDK, trace propagation via W3C traceparent header. 6. Saga pattern: choreography (event-driven) vs. orchestration (central saga orchestrator); compensating transactions. 7. Comparisons: monolith vs. microservices trade-offs, gRPC vs. REST, sync vs. async communication.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'How do you decompose a monolithic Go application into microservices?' → identify domain boundaries, extract data stores, define contracts first. • 'What happens if service B is slow and service A calls it synchronously?' → circuit breaker with sony/gobreaker, context deadline propagation, async via message queue. • 'How do you trace a request that spans five Go services?' → OpenTelemetry SDK, inject/extract trace context, send spans to Jaeger or Tempo. • 'Explain the saga pattern and when you'd use it in Go.' → distributed transaction without 2PC, choreography with Kafka events, compensating actions.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "When I decompose a monolith, I start with domain-driven design—identify bounded contexts first, then decide service boundaries. In Go, each service is a standalone binary with its own go.mod; inter-service calls use gRPC with protobuf contracts versioned in a shared proto repository. For resilience I wrap every outbound call with a context timeout and a circuit breaker using sony/gobreaker. Distributed tracing is non-negotiable: I initialise the OpenTelemetry SDK in main, inject the trace context into every outgoing gRPC or HTTP call, and ship spans to our Tempo backend. For long-running distributed transactions I prefer the saga choreography pattern with Kafka—each service publishes an event on success and a compensating event on failure—over a central orchestrator, because it avoids a single point of failure."
